fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's buying guide for landscape turf says infill helps keep turf from moving by spreading weight evenly, which minimizes its expansion and contraction as the temperature changes, and does not recommend landscape spikes in the middle of the turf in place of infill, for safety reasons.
quote: Infill is needed to help keep the synthetic grass installation from moving-infill provides an even distribution of weight that will minimize the expansion and contraction of turf when the temperature changes. For safety reasons, we do NOT recommend using landscape spikes in the middle of the synthetic grass area to replace the need for infill or top dressing ballast.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Considerations When Buying Synthetic Grass for Landscape Use (September 2013), Guidelines for Infill
notes: The PDF's text layer prints the dash after 'moving' as a hyphen; quoted as extracted. Industry trade group guidance, printed September 2013.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says turf expands as it warms and contracts as it cools, that in strong sun the hot turf pulls up from the middle into a wrinkle, and that the amount of movement depends on material quality, installation, the temperature range, the turf's age and humidity, with material quality mattering most.
quote: Just like concrete, synthetic turf expands slightly as temperature rises and contracts as temperature falls. … Thermal expansion and contraction of synthetic turf varies primarily due to quality of materials, poor installation, immediate temperature range, age of turf, and ambient relative humidity. Of these factors, the quality of materials has the greatest influence on the expansion and contraction of synthetic turf. … These wrinkles are created when the synthetic turf is exposed to extreme heat. The turf becomes hot and starts to pull from the middle uplifting, creating a wrinkle.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Thermal Expansion & Contraction in Synthetic Turf (March 2018)
notes: A turf supplier's installer column (published 2018-03-13 per the page's structured data). The column also promotes the supplier's products; the guide does not repeat that.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column calls infill ballast, the most effective way to control turf's thermal movement, says too little infill lets turf move enough to wrinkle, rupture seams or split its backing, and recommends checking each season that infill depth still meets the maker's specification.
quote: Ballast – Is the most effective way to control thermal contraction and expansion. If a sizable section of turf is not provided with proper amounts of infill to accommodate temperature movement, the synthetic turf will be allowed to move excessively which may cause wrinkling, seam rupture and/or splitting of the synthetic turf backing. … I recommend inspecting the installation every season to ensure that the infill depths are at the manufactures specifications, repairs are made and the area is kept clean of any debris.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Thermal Expansion & Contraction in Synthetic Turf (March 2018)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says putting greens are thin and very susceptible to thermal movement, that a green which shrinks or ruptures its seams has to be removed and replaced, and that infill ballast is crucial to controlling that movement.
quote: Synthetic Turf Putting Greens are very susceptible to thermal expansion and contraction. Putting green materials are not very thick in material which makes them a candidate for thermal movement. When putting greens move causing shrinkage and/or seam rupture, there is only one option, and that is to be removed and replaced. Ballast is crucial to combating thermal movement in putting greens.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Thermal Expansion & Contraction in Synthetic Turf (March 2018)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says wrinkles show less when it is cool and appear as heat makes the backing swell and lift off the ground, that turf laid early on a hot day can be too wrinkled for infill by noon, and that infill should go on once it has cooled and no wrinkles show.
quote: When the temperatures are cooler the wrinkles are less to appear. When the temperature rises, the heat transfers within the turf and causes the backing to swell and lift from the ground. This ultimately causes wrinkles. … I have been on large projects that the turf was installed early in the morning and when noon came it was too hot to place infill due to the turf having too many wrinkles. Once you start placing Infill into wrinkled turf, the chances for the Infill to weigh down the wrinkle while in its expanding/contracting mode is very slim. I recommend waiting till the temperatures lower and place the infill when there is no visible wrinkles.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Preventing Wrinkles in Turf Part 2 (June 2018)
notes: Published 2018-06-14 per the page's structured data.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's columnist says installers who don't understand why wrinkles occur leave customers unhappy, because sod doesn't wrinkle in the heat and synthetic turf shouldn't either.
quote: Inexperienced Installers that do not understand, where, when, how and why wrinkles occur, will create unhappy customers. Natural sod does not wrinkle when it gets hot so shouldn’t synthetic turf.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Preventing Wrinkles in Turf Part 2 (June 2018)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's columnist says he has seen contractors deliver 10% of the infill a turf system needed, and calls infill ballast the main defense against wrinkling.
quote: I have seen contractors deliver 10% of the Infill that is actually required to Ballast the turf system. … Placing Infill has many benefits to your turf system, not just keeping the fibers upright, but assisting in ballast which is the #1 prevention of wrinkling.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Preventing Wrinkles in Turf Part 2 (June 2018)
notes: The quote's '#1' is the columnist's; copy does not repeat it.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's columnist says turf must be lightly stretched and secured to prevent wrinkles, and that over-stretching doesn't prevent them and shortens the backing's life.
quote: You must lightly stretch and secure synthetic turf to prevent wrinkles. If you allow synthetic turf to be secured without lightly stretching, when temperatures arise you may receive wrinkles. Over stretching of the turf will not keep wrinkles at bay, in fact over stretching turf is not good for the backing and reduces its longevity.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Preventing Wrinkles in Turf Part 2 (June 2018)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's columnist says to expect wrinkles on and around slopes, mounds, sunken drains and protruding objects, where relief cuts, trimming the excess and seaming it back together may be needed.
quote: Expect there to be wrinkles when you are installing turf on and around slopes, mounds, sunken drains and protruding objects. You may have to cut reliefs, stretch out the wrinkles, cut the excess out and seam back together to remove wrinkles in these types of installations.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Preventing Wrinkles in Turf Part 2 (June 2018)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column fixes a wrinkle by removing the infill to reach the fasteners, pulling the nails or staples carefully, rolling the turf back, stretching it from one end with a carpet kicker while re-nailing, then trimming the excess and nailing the edge; it warns that fasteners rusted into the soil can tear fibers from the backing and leave divots.
quote: Prior to removing the wrinkles you must remove the infill so that you may reach the nails/staples. This is very important to successfully remove wrinkles. … When the moisture from the subgrade materials comes in contact with nails or staples that have been placed, Oxidization occurs and creates a rust/bond to the compacted soil. If you are not careful when pulling up nails or staples you will pull fibers from the backing of the turf. If this happens it will cause the surface of the turf to have “Divot” marks and you will end up replacing the entire section. … Once all the nails/staples are removed, roll the synthetic turf back to its original position. Using a carpet kicker, start at one end and stretch the turf and secure with nails/staples at the same time. … When you get to the end, you will need to cut off the excess that you have stretched out. Nail and secure edge.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Preventing Wrinkles in Turf (August 2017)
notes: Published 2017-08-17 per the page's structured data.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's installer column says that once turf has been down more than 3 months, pulling a wrinkle out may do more damage, so adding ballast or cutting the wrinkle out may be the fix, and that wrinkled turf left in sun long enough memorizes the shape and can't be stretched flat.
quote: If your turf has been down more than 3 months you may do more damage to the turf by trying to remove them. You may try to ballast or cut out the wrinkle which may rectify the problem. … If you expose wrinkled synthetic turf to UV sunlight and other harsh environmental conditions for long periods of time, this will cause the synthetic turf to memorize its shape and therefore will be impossible to remove.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Preventing Wrinkles in Turf (August 2017)

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse's columnist says coated turf backing still stretches by inches, that turf laid down as-is won't stay flat, and that slack not stretched out in winter shows up in summer heat.
quote: Even with the coating applied, the turf remains flexible, stretching by inches. If you lay synthetic turf down as-is, it won’t remain flat. Over time, movement will creep in, and things will stretch, shrink, and do all sorts of weird things, causing wrinkles, ripples, and especially when the heat rises. I have always said, “What you don’t stretch out in the wintertime, will come back and haunt you in the hot summer”.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Stop Wrinkles Before They Start (January 2026)
notes: Published 2026-01-30 per the page's structured data. Between 'inches.' and 'If you lay' the page has a paragraph break only.

fact: Shaw's ShawGrass installation guidelines say to roll the turf out the day before installation so it can relax, to lay wrinkled turf flat in the sun or stretch it, to always stretch it tight to reduce wrinkling, and to plan on about 18 inches of waste because turf nearest the core may be badly wrinkled.
quote: Roll out the turf the day before installation as this will allow the panel to relax. If the synthetic turf has wrinkles, lay it flat on a flat surface in the sun or stretch. … remember that turf wrapped closest to the core may be excessively wrinkled, plan on about 18” of waste just to be on the safe side. … Always stretch synthetic turf tight to reduce wrinkling.
source_label: Shaw Industries, ShawGrass Installation Guidelines (PDF)

fact: Shaw's ShawGrass installation guidelines call for compacting the base to 95% or greater so it is smooth and firm with no bumps under the turf, and for overlapping compactor passes to minimize ridges and bumps.
quote: Continual passes over the project area are required until a compaction rate of 95% or greater is achieved. When dry, the project area should be smooth and firm to eliminate unwanted bumps under the synthetic turf. … Overlap trips with the compactor to minimize ridges and bumps.
source_label: Shaw Industries, ShawGrass Installation Guidelines (PDF)

fact: Shaw's ShawGrass installation guidelines estimate three to five pounds of sand infill per square foot on 50- to 80-ounce turf.
quote: Calculate the amount of sand infill in advance; a good estimate is three-to-five pounds of sand per square foot on 50-80 ounce turf.
source_label: Shaw Industries, ShawGrass Installation Guidelines (PDF)

fact: PolyTurf's landscape installation manual has turf rolled out in a sunny spot so it can expand, as a step to prevent rippling after installation, and left to relax for an hour or more in warm sun before it is fastened and pulled tight with a carpet kicker.
quote: Roll out the turf in a sunny, spacious area to allow for expansion to occur and to let the blades open up. This extra step is a preventative measure to prevent rippling after installation. … Allow the turf to relax for an hour or more in the warm sun before carrying on. This allows time for the material to open and expand. … With the end secure, pull the turf tight lengthways, using the carpet kicker to help pull it out
source_label: PolyTurf, Installation and Maintenance Instructions: Synthetic Grass for Landscaping (2015)

fact: Integriturf's installation guide has turf left a few hours in direct sun so the backing and fibers relax and flatten, then stretched out toward the perimeter with a carpet kicker to remove slack, with temporary nails placed along the way.
quote: Unroll the synthetic turf and let it sit for a few hours in direct sunlight to allow the backing and fibers to relax and flatten out. … Stretch the turf outward towards the perimeter using a carpet kicker to stretch the turf out removing any slack. Place temporary nails in the turf as you work your way outward towards the edges.
source_label: Integriturf, Synthetic Turf Installation Guide (PDF)

fact: Watersavers Turf's installation guide has turf rolled out in the sun blades down for at least 1 to 2 hours to acclimate, then stretched to remove wrinkles, a carpet kicker helping, because turf expands and contracts in hot and cold weather; it warns that nails driven too far into the base leave a noticeable dip.
quote: Helpful Tip: Before installing synthetic turf, roll it out in the sun with blades facing down for at least 1 – 2 hours. This will allow the turf to acclimate and make it easier to work with. … it is critical that you stretch the artificial turf to remove any wrinkles (a carpet kicker can be useful for this). Artificial turf expands and contracts in hot and cold weather so having a tight, secure perimeter is key. … Never drive nails into base too far because this will create a noticeable dip.
source_label: Watersavers Turf, How to Install Artificial Grass

fact: Watersavers Turf's installation guide says infill runs 1.5 to 2 pounds per square foot depending on the turf's thickness.
quote: How much infill should you use? Infill amount will vary: 1.5 – 2lbs per square foot depending on thickness of the artificial grass.
source_label: Watersavers Turf, How to Install Artificial Grass

fact: Namgrass, a UK artificial grass maker, says lines and dark patches in newly unrolled turf come from the measuring wheel at the factory and from rolling it tightly on a tube, that cool backing molds to the shape under it, and that such creases and lines are normal and easily remedied.
quote: At this stage, a mechanical measuring wheel is passed over the top of the grass to ensure alignment of the rolls. This can sometimes ruffle the fibres of the grass, and cause lines. Then, as the grass is prepared for shipping, it’s wrapped tightly round a cardboard tube, before being secured. A small amount of additional pressure can cause dark patches or lines, so when the grass is then opened at its destination, the grass looks very flat and ‘lifeless’. The backing material will also contribute to any creasing, as once cool, it will mould itself to any shape underneath it. … It is perfectly normal for creases and lines to appear, and they are easily remedied.
source_label: Namgrass, How to Remove Creases from Artificial Grass (May 2016)
notes: A UK manufacturer; used for the mechanism only. Published 2016-05-16 per the page metadata.

fact: Namgrass says wrinkles that appear after installation usually follow hot weather that softens the backing so it stretches and then cools, that a proper installation prevents them, and that an installer should be asked about a refit.
quote: Sometimes wrinkles can appear after installation. This is usually when it’s been particularly hot, causing the backing to become supple again, potentially stretching and then cooling again and leaving wrinkles. This is prevented with a proper installation, but if you do find these wrinkles occurring, contact a professional installer and they will be able to advise on a refit.
source_label: Namgrass, How to Remove Creases from Artificial Grass (May 2016)

fact: The Colorado Climate Center says Colorado has large seasonal swings and large day-to-night changes in temperature, and that the eastern plains have a large daily and seasonal temperature range.
quote: There are large seasonal swings in temperature and large day to night changes. … The climate of the plains is comparatively uniform from place to place, with characteristic features of low relative humidity, abundant sunshine, infrequent rains and snow, moderate to high wind movement, and a large daily and seasonal range in temperature.
source_label: Colorado Climate Center (Colorado State University), Climate of Colorado

fact: NOAA's 1991–2020 monthly normals give an average daily temperature range (high minus low) in April, July, September and January of 30.6, 32.3, 33.2 and 26.6°F at Greeley UNC; 27.0, 28.7, 29.4 and 26.6°F at Fort Collins; 31.9, 33.5, 34.8 and 31.0°F at Loveland 2N; and 30.9, 35.5, 34.4 and 30.1°F at Longmont 2 ESE; Greeley UNC's average July high and low are 91.7 and 59.3°F.
quote: MLY-DUTR-NORMAL (Apr · Jul · Sep · Jan) — USC00053553 GREELEY UNC 30.6 · 32.3 · 33.2 · 26.6 | USC00053005 FT COLLINS 27.0 · 28.7 · 29.4 · 26.6 | USC00055236 LOVELAND 2N 31.9 · 33.5 · 34.8 · 31.0 | USC00055116 LONGMONT 2 ESE 30.9 · 35.5 · 34.4 · 30.1 — USC00053553 Jul MLY-TMAX-NORMAL 91.7 · MLY-TMIN-NORMAL 59.3
source_label: NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020, monthly, four Northern Colorado stations (daily temperature range)
notes: Values read from the NCEI access-services API on 2026-09-25. NCEI's monthly normals documentation (Normals_MLY_Documentation_1991-2020.pdf) defines mly-dutr-normal as the 'Long-term monthly mean of daily temperature range'. These are air temperatures in a standard shelter, not turf surface temperatures. Station-to-town assignment follows the shared climate.json records (nearest station, an inference); say 'the nearest NOAA station'.
